images.caption: Figure 3:Representative training data pairs across editing tasks.We show source and target video examples from our three data-generation pipelines. The pixel-aligned pipeline covers add, remove, appearance change, swap, stylization, and environment change; the localization pipeline covers highlighting, outlining, and color filling; and the semi-pixel-aligned pipeline covers environment change, medium change, and character appearance change.Note: Faces of real actors in the displayed examples are blurred to protect their identity.

Figure 4:Long-horizon appearance-drift stress test.We compare autoregressive editing with and without draft conditioning in a small-scale train setting.
Naive autoregressive editing accumulates appearance drift and saturation, while draft-conditioned rollout maintains a stable edited appearance.

Figure 5:Cascaded modeling for a long-form video editor.MoviEdit uses a shared denoiserfθf_{\theta}to first produce a globally consistent, lightweight edit on a subsampled video sequence (Draft Editor), and then propagates the edit chunk by chunk to the full-resolution video while mitigating long-horizon appearance drift (Render Editor).

Figure 6:Example source videos from MoviEdit-Bench.The examples highlight the diversity of subject composition, cross-shot grounding difficulty, and visual appearance in the benchmark. Full videos are available on our project page.
Figure 7:Qualitative comparison on MoviEdit-Bench with representative baselines.
Figure 8:MoviEdit-Bench radar chart showing that MoviEdit achieves performance on par with proprietary systems.
Figure 9:MoviEdit naturally extends to video set-to-set editing setup.

Figure 11:Ablation of task-specific data recipes.Top:Adding semi-pixel-aligned training data improves generalization to edits involving relatively larger changes in structure or shape.Bottom:Adding subject localization training data improves the model’s ability to identify the intended edit target, leading to improved edit localization.

Figure 12:Failure cases of MoviEdit.(a)Inter-subject identity ambiguity.When multiple visually similar subjects are present, the model may mistakenly apply the edit to an unintended subject rather than the specified target.
(b)Partial-observation ambiguity.When the target is only partially visible, the model may struggle to accurately localize and edit the intended subject.

Figure 13:Examples of synchronized multi-camera footage used as raw data for MoviEdit.Each scene is captured simultaneously from 2–4 cameras, showing the same real-world scene from different viewpoints while actors perform natural interactions.Note: Faces of real actors in the displayed examples are blurred to protect their identity.

Figure 14:Qualitative comparison across overall edit success scores.Representative V2V results from multiple models, ordered by overall edit success.
Examples progress from incorrect localization or incomplete edits to successful, cross-shot-consistent editing.

Figure 15:Beyond-training-horizon editing.Qualitative results on 25-second videos: (a) a 17-shot multi-shot sequence and (b) a continuous single-shot sequence. Both exceed the 15-second training horizon, demonstrating generalization to longer multi-shot and long-take videos.
